Inflammation and infection
Cystectomy for bilateral thigh fistulation after salvage radiotherapy for 
prostate cancer: A case report
B.J. Stewart a,*, S.P. McCombie a,b, D. Hayne a,b
a Fiona Stanley Hospital, 11 Robin Warren Dr, Murdoch, WA, 6150, Australia b UWA Medical School, University of Western Australia, 35 Stirling Highway, Crawley, WA, 6009, Australia
ARTICLE INFO
Keywords:
Cystectomy
Prostate cancer
Fistula
Urinary diversion
Radiotherapy
ABSTRACT
Fistulation following radiotherapy for prostate cancer is a rare occurrence that can have devastating consequences and often occurs after instrumentation. We present a 74-year-old male who underwent cystectomy for 
bilateral thigh fistulation years after radical prostatectomy and salvage radiotherapy for prostate cancer. MRI and 
CT cystogram confirmed fistulation from the anterior bladder tracking to bilateral thigh collections. Formal 
urinary diversion was performed with cystectomy and ileal conduit. Pubic or thigh pain, the inability to walk or 
evidence of local wound infection in someone who has previously had prostate radiotherapy, should alert the 
clinician to the possible presence of urethral fistulation.
1. Introduction
Fistulation following radiotherapy for prostate cancer is a rare 
occurrence that can have devastating consequences.1 Urethral instrumentation, whether intermittent self-catheterisation or during transurethral operative intervention, is often an antecedent provoking 
event.2 Urinary diversion is the mainstay of treatment, which may 
include percutaneous nephrostomies or construction of an ileal 
conduit.3 We examine the clinical course of a male in his seventies who 
underwent cystectomy and ileal conduit urinary diversion for bilateral 
thigh collections from urinary fistulation secondary to historic prostate 
radiotherapy.
2. Case presentation

A 74-year-old male presented with right thigh pain and lethargy two 
weeks after a covid-19 infection, with the initial diagnosis suspected to 
be a myositis in view of an elevated Creatine Kinase of 255. He had a 
background of having undergone a radical prostatectomy eleven years 
ago and subsequent salvage radiotherapy resulting in an undetectable 
PSA. Of note, he had a long-standing history of clean intermittent selfdilatation for an anastomotic stricture, and recently underwent a cystolitholapaxy for a bladder stone that was identified after he reported 
difficulty in self-catheterisation with associated haematuria. The only 
other biochemical abnormality was an elevated C-reactive protein of 
237, with no leucocytosis and normal renal function.
An indwelling urethral catheter was inserted and the patient underwent Magnetic Resonance Imaging that demonstrated a left thigh 
collection [Fig. 1]. Ultrasound-guided aspiration of the thigh collection 
was performed and Proteus Mirabilis, with minimal antibiotic resistance, was cultured in all urine and thigh cultures. CT cystogram 
confirmed fistulation from the anterior vesico-urethral junction tracking 
to bilateral thigh collections [Figs. 2 and 3]. Acute sepsis was managed 
with temporising bilateral percutaneous nephrostomies with concomitant intravenous antibiotics in liaison with the Infectious Diseases team. 
During this admission, cystoscopy was performed with direct visualisation of a two-centimetre defect in the anterior bladder wall immediately proximal to the vesico-urethral anastomosis. Biopsies were taken 
at the bladder neck and edge of the fistula opening, with the histopathology returning as benign with active inflammation.
A repeat outpatient MRI demonstrated progressive osteomyelitis 
despite prolonged antibiotics, urinary diversion and catheterisation. The 
decision was therefore taken three months after his initial presentation 
to proceed with a cystectomy, ileal conduit and debridement of the 
pubic symphysis osteomyelitis. Microbiology of the pubic symphysis

debridement grew Pseudomonas Aeruginosa and Enterococcus Faecium. 
Organism-directed antibiotics were continued for six weeks as guided by 
the Infectious Diseases team. His post-operative course was uncomplicated, and histopathology confirmed benign fistulation. Follow-up was

3. Discussion
Fistulation following radiotherapy, whether as a primary intervention or as ‘salvage’ treatment after prostatectomy, is a rare but devastating complication.1 The most frequent presentations of a urinary 
fistula to the skin or musculoskeletal structures of the pelvis is pubic 
pain, urinary leak via the fistulous tract, and wound infection. In a series 
of 31 men over 10 years, one third were wheelchair-bound secondary to 
pain, which sometimes led to misdiagnosis and delay in appropriate 
treatment.3 In the same series, 58 % of anterior fistula complications 
following radiotherapy were within a few months of a likely inciting 
endoscopic intervention. Matsushita et al. reported all 12 men in a series 
presenting with pubovesical fistulae had received treatment for bladder 
neck contractures following radical prostatectomy and radiotherapy.2
Identification of urinary fistulation is often by fluoroscopic or 
contrast-enhanced CT. Soft tissue delineation with MRI identifying the 
fistula tract and surrounding tissue damage has been suggested as the

new gold standard.4 Cystography remains widely available, complimenting cystoscopy and biopsy to exclude malignancy. Standard management includes culture-sensitive antibiotics, source control often with 
drainage of the collection, and temporary urinary diversion with catheterisation with or without bilateral nephrostomy insertion. Consultation with specialty colleagues is often required. Orthopaedic surgeons 
aggressively currete the pubis until soft, infected tissue is removed. 
Plastic surgeons, if necessary, reconstruct soft tissue structures. Infectious disease physicians direct organ-sensitive antimicrobial therapy.
Conservative management is often drawn out, unsuccessful and results in a poor quality of life.5 Urinary diversion with an ileal conduit is 
the most definitive option but often not suitable in the acute setting. 
Osterberg et al. proposed a guideline to help determine whether fistula 
repair or diversion with an ileal conduit may be more appropriate based 
on varying individual factors; comorbidities, distal stricture disease, 
continence and bladder capacity.3 In this study of 31 males, 30 and 
90-day post-operative complications were similar for both approaches. 
Four patients had clavien-dindo 3 infectious complications; two within 
30 days and two within 90 days. 18 of 31 patients suffered 
Clavien-Dindo Scores two or less, mostly related to post-operative ileus. 
One patient progressed to cystectomy after reoccurrence of the fistula 17 
months after primary repair. Primary repair of the urethra is considered 
if reasonable bladder capacity and a patent distal urethra exists. Risk of 
recurrence and incontinence are considerations in patient selection 
however outcomes are similar to ileal conduit diversion3
.
4. Conclusion
Urinary fistulae can be devastating and are often associated with 
previous prostate surgery and radiotherapy, and recent urethral 
instrumentation. In the context of previous radiotherapy, urethral 
instrumentation warrants thorough consideration, careful surgical 
technique, and considered counselling. Pubic and thigh pain, the 
inability to walk, or evidence of local wound infection, in a male who 
has previously had prostate radiotherapy and instrumentation, should

alert the clinician to the possibility of urethral fistulation. This is acutely 
managed with antibiotics, source control, and temporary urinary 
diversion with a urinary catheter or nephrostomy tubes. Definitive 
management may require fistula repair or an ileal conduit urinary 
diversion.
